description: Contract versioning lock. One row per PUBLIC contract: what it is, who owns it, which version is published, what its consumers are, and where its contract tests live. The architecture gate fails when a published contract's surface changes without its version changing. Intentionally tiny: this is not semver-as-a-framework, it is a change alarm.

breaking: removing or renaming an error code, or changing an existing code's HTTP status
changing the meaning or required shape of a request/response field
narrowing accepted input or widening required output
moving a file out of the declared public surface
patch: internal implementation changes with no surface change
policy.rule: A BREAKING change requires: major bump here, a note in docs/n8n-lego/BACKEND_LEGO.md §Contract changelog, and sign-off from every consumer listed below.
policy.preRelease: Contracts at 0.x are provisional: they may break with a minor bump, but the bump is still mandatory.

compatibilityModel.note: 0.x contracts are provisional: ^0.2.1 does NOT accept 0.3.0, because a 0.x minor is allowed to break. Consumers of a 0.x contract must be told about every minor.

policy.parentChildRule: A parent contract does NOT version-bump because a sub-LEGO changed compatibly. It bumps only when its own parent-facing surface moves. Example held by the fixtures: reference.validation 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 (additive) leaves reference.lego at 1.0.0 and reference.repository at 1.0.0. A BREAKING child change that surfaces through the parent does force a parent major bump.
policy.migrations: A contract may declare `migrations: ["1.3.0"]` — versions that need a data/state migration even though they are semver-compatible. Migration points are declared, never inferred.

A declaration is a CLAIM; this is where it becomes a COMMITMENT the rest of the system may read. Four guarantees, each proven by test rather than asserted: (1) deterministic compile — the epoch digest is a pure function of declaration CONTENT and the lineage it is compiled onto, invariant under key order, declaration order and capability order, with no clock, no filesystem and no network anywhere in the module (a compiler that reads a clock is not reproducible); (2) all-or-nothing — one invalid declaration or one duplicate identity compiles to NO epoch at all, with P6.1's own reason codes carried through unchanged (registry.duplicate keeps its 'a conflict, not a precedence rule' wording) rather than re-invented; (3) monotonic chained history — an epoch names its parent digest and carries the full chain, epoch numbers only ever increase, and a rollback is a NEW higher-numbered epoch that re-installs older content (its contentDigest equals the target's, its epochDigest does not), so a downgrade leaves a mark instead of restoring a number, and a rollback to a non-ancestor or to the current epoch is refused; (4) immutability — a compiled epoch is deep-frozen and publication is a pointer move between frozen objects, so the epoch in-flight work is reading stays bit-identical (asserted by re-serializing it) and a failed publication leaves the previous state fully usable. Also: verifyRegistryEpoch recompiles content and refuses anything whose digest no longer matches (tamper detection, with invalid content reported as invalid rather than as a mismatch); diffRegistryEpochs gives sorted added/removed/changed for P6.19. Identity, validation, canonical form and per-declaration digests are quoted from node.registry@0.1.0 — the compiler never re-derives them. No authority: compiling is not admitting. Scope walls held: no install journal, artifact store, lease, residency, health, quarantine or attestation vocabulary exists in this module.

contracts.notes: P6.3 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): transactional package install + single-flight. P6.1 fixes what a declaration IS, P6.2 compiles declarations into an epoch — neither says how a package gets from a tarball to the registry the host serves, and that gap is where the damage happens: an interrupted copy leaves a half-written package, two concurrent installs produce a mixture of both, and a rollback applied to a stale view silently undoes someone else's upgrade. This contract owns the ORDERING, the JOURNAL, the ATTEMPTS, the VISIBILITY BOUNDARY and the single-flight arbitration, and deliberately not the bytes: every step result is reported back by the caller, so the host does the IO while this contract says what a valid history looks like and refuses anything else (the same split P6.1 and P6.2 already use). Steps, in the only order they may happen: resolve → prepare → verify → stage → publish → activate, none skippable. `publish` is THE VISIBILITY BOUNDARY: before it a failure costs nothing (recovery aborts), after it the registry is inconsistent until activation completes or the publication is rolled back — a decision that is asymmetric by design and symmetric in shape (attempts left → resume; exhausted → abort before the boundary, rollback after it). Attempt numbering is EXPLICIT because 'the same failure twice' is ambiguous in a way that matters: replaying a recorded attempt is a no-op (a crashed driver must be able to reconcile its own journal, even after the transaction closed), a new attempt counts toward a ceiling of two, and a gap in attempt numbers is a lost report rather than a new attempt — an omitted number means 'next attempt', which is fail-safe, since over-counting ends a transaction while under-counting loops forever. A step that already succeeded can never be re-recorded; a journal is evidence, not a draft. Publication is FENCED: it must name the 64-hex epoch digest it makes visible (it composes with P6.2, it does not mint an epoch) and it is refused under a lease the gate no longer holds — single-flight is one install per package identity at a time, with a monotonic fence, re-entrancy for the same owner that does not burn a fence, and a stale holder having no authority over the gate. Immutable throughout: every function returns a new frozen value, so a history in front of an operator cannot change under them.

contracts.notes: P6.4 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): dependency closure + content-addressed artifact store. P6.3 gives an install a journal and a fence but installs ONE package; real node packages arrive with helpers, parsers and runtimes, so something must answer which packages are needed, in which versions, and whether the bytes on hand are the bytes the registry claims. This contract answers all three, purely. RESOLUTION: given a root and a catalogue of published versions (data handed in, never fetched), produce the full closure as a deterministic, topologically ordered list of package@version with the digest each must have — deterministic meaning two hosts resolving the same catalogue get byte-identical results, because a closure that depends on map iteration order is a coin flip, not a closure. Semver subset stated rather than imported: `*`, exact, caret and tilde over major.minor.patch with an optional pre-release, and a pre-release is never selected unless a requirement NAMES it (a caret range that happens to cover 1.1.0-beta.1 must not install a beta). STORE ADDRESSING: an address IS the hash of the content, so identical bytes share one address and cannot disagree about it — which is what makes deduplication safe rather than clever. VERIFICATION: content that no longer hashes to its address is refused as corruption and never silently re-addressed. Every refusal here has burned a real supply chain and is reported with who asked for what: unmet required dependency, unsatisfiable range (nearby versions are not picked), a version conflict no single version satisfies, a declared conflict with something the closure requires (checked AFTER the closure is complete, because whether a conflict fires depends on the whole graph), a cycle with the path named, a depth ceiling and a size ceiling. Optional means may-be-absent, never may-be-wrong: an absent optional is reported in `optionalMissing`, a declared-but-broken one is reported with its reason. Garbage collection requires the live set from the caller — collecting by guessing is data loss with a spec. No authority: an address proves identity of bytes, never authorship, trust or permission.

contracts.notes: P6.5 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): workflow node resolution manifest. An epoch (P6.2) answers what the registry contains now; it does not answer what THIS workflow runs against and whether that changed — between those two questions sits the classic outage where the registry is upgraded, half the workflows silently start executing an untested version, and the only evidence is a support ticket. A resolution manifest pins, per workflow, the exact identity (type@typeVersion), the declaration digest and the epoch digest, so 'which implementation did this run use' is a stored fact next to the workflow instead of a reconstruction. Three rules make it worth having. (1) A PIN IS EXACT: no latest, no floating tag, no silent adoption. (2) UPGRADE IS EXPLICIT AND TWO-PHASE: planning changes nothing at all (asserted by re-serializing the manifest), applying requires an explicit authorization, a revision that still matches, and a proposal that still equals what the current epoch would produce — a stale proposal is refused rather than merged, which is how an upgrade approved yesterday against a different registry stops being applied today; the policy (exact/minor/major, in the n8n typeVersion X.Y model) travels INSIDE the proposal and is recorded in history when it changes. (3) NOTHING IS SILENTLY DROPPED: a pinned identity missing from the epoch is FATAL even when a candidate version exists — turning 'the node you pinned is gone' into 'here is a different version instead' is the exact failure this contract prevents — and the same identity carrying a different digest is reported as a registry integrity violation, not an upgrade, because P6.1 fixed that a node's identity never changes because its implementation changed. Revisions only increase and history is append-only. Composes with P6.1 (identity/parse) and P6.2 (epochs) rather than re-deriving either; P3's graph, frontier and IR modules are never imported — the node list is data handed in.

contracts.notes: P6.6 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): runtime lease + side-by-side upgrade. P6.2 publishes an epoch by moving a pointer between frozen objects, which is only safe if nothing is still executing inside the old one — and something always is. 'Deploy' and 'what is running' are different questions, and the gap between them is where the upgrade outage lives: the new version is published, an in-flight execution silently switches versions half-way through, and the result is a state neither version would have produced. Three mechanisms close it. (1) LEASES: a lease names the EPOCH DIGEST the execution runs under (never a version number, never 'current'), so a later publication cannot re-point work already running; a lease id is DERIVED from execution + epoch, so a retried acquire is the same lease rather than a second one. (2) DRAIN: explicit and observable — draining immediately stops new admissions while everything inside keeps running, and returns the outstanding executions so a deploy can wait honestly. (3) RETIRE, GATED ON THE LEASES: an epoch cannot be retired while a single lease is outstanding, the refusal NAMES who is holding it, and draining must come first because retiring an epoch that is still admitting work is a race with whoever is asking for a lease right now. Side-by-side serving is the consequence rather than a feature: several epochs may serve at once (old for in-flight, new for new work) and the table reports exactly which. A retired epoch NUMBER can never be reused by different content, so a number is not a place to hide a rewrite. The table carries a monotonic SEQUENCE instead of a clock, because a lease table that reads a clock is not reproducible, and every operation returns a new frozen table so the state in front of an operator cannot change under them. No authority: a lease grants nothing but the right to keep serving the epoch it names — no trust, no capability, no permission.

contracts.notes: P6.7 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): manifest/implementation split + HOT/WARM/COLD residency. An epoch can hold hundreds of node types; a process cannot hold hundreds of loaded implementations, and pretending otherwise is how a node registry becomes a memory leak with a catalogue. The split this contract enforces is that THE MANIFEST AND THE IMPLEMENTATION ARE DIFFERENT THINGS: a declaration is cheap and needed for resolution and editing, an implementation is expensive and needed only while running. Three tiers: COLD (known to the epoch, nothing resident here), WARM (the MANIFEST is resident, the implementation is not), HOT (the implementation is resident). COLD → WARM → HOT is the ONLY way up, and that is the point — metadata is read BEFORE code is loaded, which is what leaves room for a capability, trust or residency check to happen at all; a load straight from COLD is refused rather than quietly warmed as a side effect, because the check that was skipped would never be reported (there would be nothing to report it). HOT is BOUNDED by an explicit budget: exceeding it demotes the LEAST-RECENTLY-USED node to WARM and says which one, so memory pressure is a reported policy instead of an out-of-memory kill. Eviction RESPECTS LEASES: an implementation an execution is still holding is never unloaded, `inUseBy` is a REQUIRED input, and a non-empty set refuses the eviction with the executions named; WARM → COLD is a separate ordered step (a HOT node must be evicted before its manifest is dropped). Recency is a monotonic TICK, not a timestamp, so the same operations produce the same table anywhere, and every operation returns a new frozen table. Depends only on P6.2 for epochs; the lease set is passed in as data rather than importing P6.6. No authority: being hot grants nothing and being cold revokes nothing.

contracts.notes: P6.8 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): capability compilation + runtime locality. A declaration says what a node NEEDS (P6.1: capabilities, runtime locality, resource profile); it does not say what a node GETS. This contract is that decision, made once, in one place, deterministically, so that 'why did this node run in-process?' has an answer that is a document instead of an interrogation. Three rules do the work. (1) The host is validated first, as data: which capabilities it can authorize, which runtimes it has, and the STRONGEST isolation it can offer; an unknown capability, runtime or boundary is refused, and an anonymous host or one with no runtime is refused too, because a host that cannot say what it is cannot be trusted with the decision. (2) Capabilities are GRANTED IN FULL OR THE PLAN IS REFUSED: granted = declared and host, never a reduced plan, because a node running with half its declared capabilities has failure modes nobody wrote down. (3) CAPABILITIES CONSTRAIN LOCALITY: subprocess demands at least 'sandboxed', native demands 'worker-isolated', and a host that cannot offer the floor refuses the plan and says which floor it needed — convenience is not an argument when the answer is sharing an address space. Runtime selection itself belongs to node.portability@1.0.0 and is DELEGATED, not copied; the plan quotes the domain's answer (selected target, candidates, rejected, policy). MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: the two contracts describe different capability axes — P6.1's capabilities quote the foundation's trust capabilities (network, filesystem, subprocess, secrets, native, env) while node.portability validates requiredCapabilities against the registry's own capability ids (runtime.http-server, ai.model-gateway, ...) and demands class-specific permission ids from the published registry vocabulary (webhook:receive, storage:read, worker:admin, ...). No faithful projection exists between those vocabularies, so none is fabricated: writing a declared 'network' into requiredCapabilities would be a lie that happens to compile. When the caller supplies the node's OWN portability declaration (bound to the same node, validated by the domain, refused if it belongs to a neighbour), the plan performs a REAL delegation and quotes it; when no declaration is supplied the plan records delegation.performed=false, delegation.source='none', delegation.reason='capability.delegation.none' and derives the target from RUNTIME_LOCALITY_MODEL. A plan never pretends a delegation happened. trustClass is carried as a LABEL for policy, never as an authority: it changes no decision and is excluded even from planDigest, so two nodes differing only in trust class compile to the same decision AND the same fingerprint of that decision. Scope walls: no leases or attenuation (P6.22), no admission decision, no quarantine (P6.11) and no attestation (P6.12), no sandbox, worker, pool or process (P6.24), and no filesystem, network, clock, randomness or mutation.

contracts.notes: P6.9 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): semantic fingerprint + compatibility replay. A node version is a claim — 'same node, same contract' — and the cheap check (comparing bytes) answers a different question: two artifacts can differ in every byte and still be the same node, and one artifact can differ in one character and behave differently forever. So this contract fingerprints the CONTRACT, not the artifact, over nine axes: type, typeVersion, parameters, expressions, credentials, io, webhooks, behavior, ui. Everything that describes how a node is SUPPLIED or GOVERNED (implementation digest and language, packageVersion, provenance, trustClass, health, lifecycle) is recorded beside the fingerprint and never inside it, because the implementation language is not part of the contract: a node reimplemented from JavaScript in Rust is the same node, and a replay reports implementationChanged: true while still saying MATCH. Canonicalisation is the precondition for a fingerprint at all: keys are sorted, unordered axes (credentials, io, webhooks) are compared as sets, and anything that cannot be canonicalised — a function, an undefined, a non-finite number, a Symbol, a BigInt, a Map/Set/class instance, a cycle — makes the answer NON_DETERMINISTIC with the offending path and kind named, because a hash over a guess would look like an answer. An axis a node does not declare is recorded as ABSENT rather than empty: 'no credentials' and 'credentials were not declared' are different claims and only one of them is safe to replay. Replay has four answers and no fifth: MATCH (semantics identical, implementation may not be), DIFF (semantics changed, with the worst axis deciding the impact on the ladder none < cosmetic < compatible < behavioral < breaking, plus at most 32 path-addressed leaf changes and an explicit truncation flag), NON_DETERMINISTIC (no fingerprint exists) and MISSING (no baseline: an absent fingerprint is never a match). ok means the replay could be PERFORMED, not that the answer was good: a DIFF is an answer, NON_DETERMINISTIC and MISSING are refusals to answer. Fingerprints can also be replayed without the semantics they came from (the worker handshake and the cache exchange fingerprints), and an unverifiable fingerprint is treated as a missing baseline. Scope walls: no admission decision (P6.11), no quarantine, no lifecycle transition (P6.10), no migration/repair (P6.30), no artifact or source inspection, no clock, no network, no randomness, no mutation — the only node import is the hash.

contracts.notes: P6.10 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): orphan / tombstone / alias / deprecation. An epoch is a set of identities; what it cannot say is what has been removed, renamed, abandoned, and which names must never come back — and the cost of not saying it is a name that gets re-used. A lifecycle LEDGER is built for one epoch: every identity starts 'declared', every transition returns a NEW frozen ledger (the old one is untouched), and the ledger digest makes an edited ledger visible. ORPHAN: a node nobody references is a report, never an automatic uninstall, and it is reported together with the mirror-image fact that matters more — a reference nobody provides, which is a workflow that cannot resolve. DEPRECATION: a node still resolves and still runs, must name a replacement the epoch actually contains (a redirect to nowhere is refused), and records the epoch it happened at. ALIAS: one hop only, and only for a name that has been retired (deprecated or disabled) — a chain of redirects is a rename nobody can audit, and an alias to a tombstone is refused. TOMBSTONE: the single irreversible thing here. It records its grounds (removed, renamed, compromised, superseded, policy), it cannot be edited, the state cannot move afterwards, nothing may alias to it, and mayReuseName says false — because a tombstoned identity can never be re-declared, and the cost of that rule is a naming decision made twice while the cost of the alternative is an attacker who waits. Everything else is reversible on purpose: registries are governed by people who change their minds. The state vocabulary is QUOTED from P6.1 (which quotes the P2 negotiation contract: eleven words, 'deprecated' among them); this contract adds events and records, never a twelfth word. Scope walls: no admission or health decision (P6.11), no quarantine, no workflow resolution (P6.5), no install/uninstall (P6.3), no catalog or database read, no clock — atEpoch is data the caller supplies, which is what makes a ledger reproducible. Pure: the only node import is the hash.

contracts.notes: P6.11 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): health + crash circuit breaker + quarantine. A node that crashed once is a fact; a node that crashes every time is a decision, and this contract is the smallest defensible version of it. The state vocabulary is P6.1's (unknown, healthy, degraded, failing, quarantined), quoted rather than extended; what this contract adds is the transition rules between those words. OBSERVATION: success or failure with a tick the caller supplies — no clock, so a table rebuilt from the same ticks produces the same states and a quarantine survives a restart instead of being a memory in a process. DERIVATION: the state follows from the observations, never the reverse. BREAKER: consecutive failures (default threshold 3, configurable) open the circuit, and mayServe refuses work with the tick at which a probe may be tried; after the cool-off exactly one probe is allowed (half-open), a success closes the circuit, and a failure re-opens it with a doubled cool-off bounded at MAX_COOL_OFF_TICKS so a permanently broken node stays visible instead of vanishing into an unbounded back-off. A success recorded BEFORE the cool-off is data, not a verdict: it is recorded and the circuit stays open, because a success that was not allowed to happen proves nothing. QUARANTINE: the deliberate version of the same thing — it records origin (operator/breaker/policy/attestation), reason and tick; it outranks every observation (a success does not clear it, and a second, different quarantine is refused as 'released, not overwritten'); it does not expire. RELEASE returns the node to 'unknown', never to 'healthy': the only thing that makes a node healthy is an observation that says so, and a release that returned to healthy would be an operator's optimism wearing a state machine's clothes. Scope walls: no execution and no retry (mayServe decides whether a retry is allowed and leaves the retrying to the runtime), no lease (P6.6), no residency (P6.7), no capability (P6.8), no lifecycle (P6.10), no revocation (P6.12), no rollback (P6.19); no clock; the only node import is the hash.

contracts.notes: P6.12 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): supply-chain attestation + revocation + offline mirror. An artifact digest answers 'is this the same bytes?' and nothing else; this contract asks the next question — who says so, about what, and may they? STATEMENT: a builder attests a predicate (build-provenance, source-review, vulnerability-scan, reproducible-build, ai-generation) about a subject digest, issued at a tick and optionally expiring. SIGNATURE: the statement is bound to its own bytes by an HMAC-SHA256 digest over the statement without its signature, computed with a key the CALLER holds (the registry never signs on anyone's behalf; signAttestation exists so verification is testable and so a builder inside the platform has a defined way to speak). POLICY: which builders may attest which packages (explicit ['*'] is a decision, never an omission) and which predicates; anonymous policies and unrestricted builders are refused; requiredPredicates make an attestation mandatory. THE TWO FAILURES STAY SEPARATE: 'the signature does not cover these bytes' and 'this builder was never allowed to assert this' are different answers, and collapsing them into one boolean is how a supply-chain check becomes a formality — which is why reports carry reasons[], a primaryReason chosen by an explicit priority (revoked > signature > subject > window > builder > statement > predicate) and a message. FAIL CLOSED: allowUnattested defaults to false and an absent attestation is a refusal; where an operator allows an exemption, the decisions are marked unattested: true and the mirror report says so, so the exemption is visible in the report instead of invisible in the behaviour. REVOCATION IS THE ONE-WAY DOOR: artifacts and builders are revoked separately, revocation is idempotent, re-revoking with a different reason is refused ('evidence is not edited'), there is no unrevoke, and revocation is checked on the SUBJECT — a probe found that an artifact with no attestations at all never reached the revocation check, which is exactly the case an exemption would wave through, so verifyAttestations now checks the subject digest itself. OFFLINE MIRROR: a mirror is DATA (id, source, artifacts with digests and attestations, and a manifest digest); verifyMirror verifies it with exactly the same policy because being offline is not a reason to accept something, and the exemption never beats revocation or a failed check. Scope walls: no signing on behalf of others, no asymmetric PKI or certificate chains, no TUF freshness (P6.28) and no transparency log (P6.27), no network or mirror transport, no artifact store (P6.4), no health (P6.11), no lifecycle (P6.10), no clock.

contracts.notes: P6.13 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): incremental registry compilation + discovery/runtime split. registry.compiler@0.1.0 (P6.2) compiles an epoch from a full declaration set — correct for a genesis epoch, wasteful for the tenth one. This is a NEW contract rather than a minor bump to the compiler, deliberately: the compiler's job ('given declarations, produce the canonical epoch') did not change, and adding an export to a locked row would have meant re-versioning a contract every consumer cites for no semantic change. What is added is a different job: given a previous epoch and a desired declaration set, produce the next epoch while PROVING it is the same epoch a full compile would have produced. THE EQUIVALENCE IS THE CONTRACT: applyRegistryChanges returns the epoch plus a reuse ledger (added/recompiled/reused/removed) that asserts byte-for-byte digest stability for reused identities, and verifyIncremental recompiles from scratch and compares epochDigest — an optimisation that cannot be verified is a guess with better latency. planRegistryChanges makes the change set a VALUE a human can review before anything is built (and refuses duplicates honestly instead of letting a plan hide one). An unchanged set is refused ('registry.incremental.unchanged') because an epoch identical to its parent is noise. Removals are data about an epoch, never a tombstone: retiring a NAME permanently is P6.10's decision. THE DISCOVERY/RUNTIME SPLIT: one epoch, two projections with their own digests — DISCOVERY carries identity, type, typeVersion, displayName, group, description, capabilities and trustClass and NEVER the implementation digest or the resource profile; RUNTIME carries identity, content digest, runtime locality, capabilities and the resource profile and NEVER the display metadata. A view is a projection, never the epoch: verifyEpochView rebuilds the projection and refuses a view that cannot be rebuilt, so nobody can present half an epoch as the whole one. contracts.notes: P6.14 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): worker registry convergence + handshake. A worker that is behind is a fact; a worker that is WRONG is a different fact, and a registry that cannot tell them apart has two bad options (bring everything forward blindly, or refuse everything). FOUR DECISIONS AND NO FIFTH: MATCH (holds exactly this epoch and its reported runtime view), UPGRADE_REQUIRED (behind AND consistent — holds a subset with matching digests under a lower epoch number), MISMATCH (holds something this registry does not: an identity the epoch lacks, a digest that disagrees for a shared identity, or a higher epoch number than the coordinator), UNAVAILABLE (the coordinator has nothing to converge TO — an epoch that is not serving, or none at all). THE MISMATCH RULE IS THE POINT: 'behind' is a position and 'divergent' is a claim that disagrees; the first is a scheduling problem and the second is a correctness or supply-chain problem, and collapsing them gives the dangerous one the treatment of the harmless one — so divergence is checked BEFORE lag and a single disagreement outranks any amount of being behind. A HIGHER EPOCH NUMBER IS NOT AN UPGRADE: quiet convergence onto an older epoch would rewrite a worker's history without asking why it was ahead, so it is escalated. MATCH requires the epoch AND the REPORTED runtime view to agree (P6.13's view digest): 'no view reported' is a question, not an agreement, because a worker that cannot state its view digest cannot be keyed by a pool or a compiled cache. CONVERGENCE IS A PLAN, NOT A TRANSPORT: decisions carry ordered steps (request-runtime-view, request-full-epoch, apply-registry-changes, reverify-views, refuse-service, escalate-to-operator, retry-when-serving) and the contract stops there; a view-only upgrade does not tell the worker to apply changes it already holds. Epoch digests are accepted bare (as registry.compiler publishes them) or prefixed, and stored in the epoch's own form so a comparison needs no translation. Scope walls: no compile or publish (P6.2/P6.13), no transport (no network, queue or socket), no lease (P6.6), no loading (P6.7), no capability (P6.8), no health (P6.11), no pooling (P6.24), no repair (P6.30); no clock, no randomness, no mutation — the only node import is the hash.

Fourteen contracts, fourteen promises; this contract is the one that CHECKS them, because 'we wrote tests' is not the same claim as 'the core behaves as specified, on demand, with evidence'. A CLAIM IS A SENTENCE AND A RUNNER: the sentences live in ACCEPTANCE_CLAIMS (id, category, statement, covers) and the runners drive the REAL contracts through their public surface — no mocks, no stubs, no private imports — so a claim cannot pass while the contract is broken. contracts.notes: P6.16 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): registry integrity chain + freshness/anti-rollback. P6.2 compiles epochs and P6.13 makes them cheap; neither answers the question a client asks before serving anything: is this the registry, and is it the newest one I should believe? THE CHAIN: each epoch becomes a LINK {index, epochNumber, epochDigest, origin, source, parentLinkDigest, linkDigest}; a link's digest covers its own fields plus the previous link's digest, so rewriting one link rewrites every link after it and a rewrite is DETECTED rather than argued about. THREE REFUSALS: monotonic (a number that does not increase is refused, and a number that reappears with different bytes is a FORK rather than a lag), continuity (an epoch that declares a parent must declare THIS head), and idempotent re-append (changed:false), because a retrying replicator must not be able to grow a chain by accident. A RECOVERY EPOCH IS NOT A ROLLBACK: P6.2's rule is quoted, a rollback is a NEW epoch carrying older content, so its number increases and the chain accepts it while its origin records what it is. ANTIBOLLBACK IS A CLIENT PROPERTY: a server cannot tell that it is old, so checkFreshness takes a WITNESS (the highest epoch a client has seen plus its link digest and chain digest) and answers three states and no fourth — current (with behindBy), rollback (the chain is older, the witnessed link is gone, or the history was rewritten), unknown (no recall). unknown FAILS CLOSED: a client with no recall cannot detect a rollback, so the caller must say firstContact:true out loud. A PROBE FOUND A REAL HOLE: a witness names the head, so a chain edited BEHIND the head was not caught by the witness alone — checkFreshness now verifies the chain first and refuses a broken chain outright, because an exception accepts an older registry and never a corrupt one; a fully resealed forgery (every later link and the chain digest rebuilt) is still caught by the witness as a rewritten history. A ROLLBACK CAN BE ACCEPTED, ON THE RECORD: reason, actor and tick, recorded in its own field, so 'we rolled back' is a decision somebody made rather than a drift nobody noticed. AN EMPTY CHAIN: nothing to witness, nothing to check freshness against. contracts.notes: P6.18 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): SBOM/VEX + policy diff gate. An epoch is an executable description nobody outside the registry can read, and two questions get asked in every serious review: what exactly is in here, and what changed and is that allowed? AN SBOM IS A READING OF AN EPOCH, never a second source of truth: one record per package version carrying the checksums of the node declarations it provides, the trust classes present, the capability names asked for, the licence as declared by the caller (NOASSERTION when nobody said), and DEPENDENCIES SUPPLIED FROM P6.4's closure rather than invented (an epoch lists nodes, not edges, and a document that invented edges would be a second registry). The format is SPDX-SHAPED so a consumer does not learn a dialect, and it is NAMED lego-sbom@1 rather than claiming a conformance it has not been tested against. A DIFF NAMES THE FIELDS THAT CHANGED (added/removed/changed with the changed fields listed, plus trustDirection and capabilityDelta): 'it changed' is how a review becomes a rumour. THE TRUST LADDER IS P6.1'S, QUOTED: exactly the four classes, ordered untrusted < community < verified < core, unknown names refused — and because P6.1 declares trust PER DECLARATION, a package can hold two classes, so the document records the SET and comparisons use the WEAKEST member (design fix found by the first suite run: refusing such an epoch would make the document useless for exactly the registries it exists to describe). VEX IS AN ATTRIBUTED STATEMENT: a status, a justification from a closed list, the actor and the tick; 'not_affected' demands a justification; two statements disagreeing about one vulnerability in one package are refused rather than ordered; and where nobody said anything the rollup stays 'under_investigation', which is not a pass. The package rollup is the status that most needs attention (affected > under_investigation > fixed > not_affected) and the statements travel with the package so a reader sees evidence rather than a summary. THE GATE IS POLICY AS DATA: rules declared by id and kind (no-new-packages, no-removals, no-new-capabilities, no-trust-downgrade, max-added-packages, no-affected-vulnerability), a policy with no rules or an unknown kind or a duplicated id is refused, and a rule whose evidence is missing yields INCOMPLETE — a gate that opens because it could not look is not a gate. Authority: an allowed diff is permission to proceed with a change, never a claim that the result is safe.

contracts.notes: P6.19 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): canary rollout, side-by-side upgrade, rollback. An upgrade is a change to what runs, and the only honest way to make it is side by side: TWO EPOCHS STAY RESOLVABLE AT ONCE, a declared share of work moves to the candidate, and the stop condition is checked rather than assumed. A rollout with a single stage is REFUSED as a cutover (that is not a canary), shares must strictly grow and the last stage must reach the whole share (a rollout that stops short leaves two epochs serving forever). ASSIGNMENT IS MONOTONE: a key is a bucket of the rollout id and salt, the bucket is fixed for the life of the rollout, and stage shares are cumulative, so a key that reached the candidate NEVER COMES BACK — an execution flapping between epochs would be a bug reported as a flake. Observations are DATA from other contracts (P6.11's health state, P6.10's lease counts), never imported verdicts; the health vocabulary is quoted from node.health, not re-declared. A stage that cannot be evaluated HALTS: no observations, an unknown health state, an attempts count missing or below the floor — `unknown` is not a synonym for `fine`, and a failure rate without a denominator is an opinion. The failure ceiling is a boundary (exactly at the ceiling advances, above it halts) and a stage may declare a stricter one. Halts carry a rule from a CLOSED LIST plus a reason and a tick, because a free-text reason makes 'why did we stop' unanswerable six months later; a second halt on the same rollout is refused rather than appended (found by the suite: without the guard the record could be rewritten). ROLLBACK IS A STATE, NOT AN UNDO: it returns new work to the previous epoch, RETAINS the candidate (digest, epoch number, stage and share at halt) and reports how many executions are still draining, because draining is not abandoning. A rolled-back or halted rollout is never reopened and cannot be completed; continuing is a new rollout with a new id and fresh evidence. Completion is the only claim a rollout makes, and it requires the last stage, an evaluation that says advance, and a previous epoch with nothing left held. Authority: this contract routes new work during a rollout; a completed rollout is a record of what happened, never a claim that the candidate was safe.

contracts.notes: P6.20 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): emergency revocation bulletins. Normal change reaches the runtime through epochs (compiled, hash-linked, witnessed in P6.13/P6.16); a security emergency cannot wait for that path, and the whole difficulty is keeping the other channel from becoming a second registry with weaker rules. A BULLETIN BINDS TO A BASELINE EPOCH DIGEST, so it is dated evidence about a specific registry state; applying it to an OLDER epoch is refused, because a change cannot be un-seen by going back. It is OFF-BAND, NOT OUT-OF-CONTROL: bulletins carry a monotone sequence and their own client-side witness, so a replayed or forked bulletin is refused by a client that has seen a newer one WITHOUT asking the registry, and a witness that has not declared its first contact FAILS CLOSED (it cannot tell a replay from a first bulletin). TIME-BOXED AUTHORITY IS NOT TIME-BOXED EFFECT: a bulletin is pending, active or lapsed at a tick and the window is bounded (a standing policy is refused and told to use the durable path) — BUT A LAPSED BULLETIN KEEPS DENYING until somebody disposes of it, because an emergency that silently expires is a rollback nobody decided. UPHOLDING MUST LAND SOMEWHERE DURABLE (`durableRef` required: this contract denies work, it does not make a revocation permanent), and lifting is recorded with an actor, a reason and a tick. The single decision is `decideSubject`, and its only path to `allow` is that nothing in the channel names the subject: an unreadable sequence denies the subjects it names while still allowing subjects it does not (the denial is narrow on purpose), and an unknown subject kind is refused rather than cleared. First suite run found two real defects, both fixed: (1) a chain compared by raw string reported a correctly linked bulletin as `unlinked` because `normalizeDigest` prefixes while `bulletinDigest` is bare — two spellings of one digest now compare as one digest; (2) a sequence starting in the middle (an orphan) crashed the comparison against a null predecessor instead of being REPORTED as `orphan`. Subjects are identities (`type@typeVersion`), package versions or artifact digests, and the two digest spellings of P6.2 address one subject. Authority: a bulletin denies work; it never grants it and never repairs a registry.

contracts.notes: P6.21 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): the node I/O compiler. A declaration says what a node reads and writes; that is the part of the contract a workflow is wired to and the part that breaks quietly when a version moves or a node moves between runtimes. The compiler turns ports into an ENFORCEABLE WIRE CONTRACT: named ports (one name per direction, so a name is one wire), connection types QUOTED FROM N8N'S PUBLISHED VOCABULARY (`main` plus the twelve `ai_*` types; the documentation's `ai_vectorRetriever` is accepted as an ALIAS and compiled to `ai_vectorStore` with `aliasedFrom` recorded, because guessing which spelling a real workflow uses is exactly the guessing this milestone refuses to do), typed item fields, and a digest per shape so a change in a promise is visible without reading it. A node that neither reads nor writes is refused, and a node with no input must be a trigger — otherwise nothing can ever reach it. COMPATIBILITY IS A VERDICT WITH REASONS: `compareNodeIo` answers identical / additive / breaking and names each change (port-removed, connection-type-changed, arity-narrowed, field-removed, field-type-changed, field-added, shape-closed, trigger-changed). Whether a new field is breaking depends on the shape NOW: a field added to a shape that is closed is breaking because every producer must supply it, while the same field added to an open shape is additive (this distinction was sharpened after the first suite run, where a closed→open move was reported breaking for the wrong reason). A HANDOFF IS ANSWERED PER FIELD: moving a node between `js-compat`, `wasm`, `rust-native` and `remote-worker` (the foundation's four localities, quoted) gives every field an inline, reference or refused transport. A BINARY PAYLOAD NEVER CROSSES INLINE: it travels as a HANDLE into the artifact store that the host resolves on the far side, because a payload is not pushed into another runtime. A `date` is REFUSED across a boundary — it is an object, not a value, and the compiler will not promise it arrives intact — and the plan fails closed with the refused fields named. Within one locality the early answer is 'nothing crosses'. contracts.notes: P6.22 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): just-in-time leases for runtime slots. A worker does not hold every implementation it might be asked to run: it holds slots and fills them when work arrives, which is what keeps memory bounded and what makes a cold start a decision rather than an accident. A LEASE NAMES WHAT IT IS FOR — identity, the wire contract digest it was granted against (P6.21's, passed as data) and the worker's locality (the foundation's four, quoted) — so a lease granted for one wire contract is refused rather than reused once the digest moves. SLOTS ARE THE RESOURCE AND THEY COME BACK BY THEMSELVES: capacity is per worker, and a slot is NOT held by a lease that has already expired even if nobody has swept it yet, so a request lazily expires what is dead before counting what is live (a host that refuses work because of its own bookkeeping is a host that lies; suite case: two expired leases free their slots with no explicit reap, and the record still shows them as expired). AN IDLE LEASE CANNOT BE RENEWED: renewal requires a use since the last renewal, because a slot held with paperwork is a leak, and the refusal says so ('let it expire'). A JIT LEASE IS SHORT BY CONSTRUCTION: time to live, total life from grant (120-tick ceiling) and renewals are all bounded, and a renewal that would outlive the ceiling is refused with the deadline named. EXPIRY IS NOT DELETION: the record keeps who held a slot, for what, uses and when it lapsed, so releasing a lapsed lease is bookkeeping that reports 'the slot came back on its own' rather than a second event, while releasing twice is REFUSED because it would count one slot twice. Requesting the same (identity, wire contract) twice hands back the lease that exists instead of a second slot. A request that does not fit is refused with `jit.capacity` and never queued: queueing is the scheduler's decision, and a contract that quietly held requests would be a scheduler with no policy. First suite run found a real defect: the worker terms were frozen together with the live bookkeeping record, so the first grant threw on assigning the lease counter — terms are now frozen and returned as a descriptor while the stored record stays live. A second defect of ordering was fixed by decision: an invalid `ttl` argument now throws before any state check, because a caller's mistake must be reported as one however the lease happens to be standing. Scope walls: no scheduling or queueing (P4), no epoch execution leases (P6.10 — an epoch lease and a slot lease are different promises), no health judgement (P6.11), no admission decision (P6.17), no cache (P6.26), no pools (P6.24); no filesystem, network, clock or randomness — every answer takes the tick it answers for, and the only node import is the hash. Authority: this contract decides whether a slot may be used, for how long and for what; it never decides whether a node should run and never loads anything.

contracts.notes: P6.23 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): cancellation and accounting. Cancellation is the moment a runtime is most likely to lie — work that was asked to stop and did not is reported as stopped, a slot that is still held is declared free, a result that arrived after the cancel is quietly dropped — and this contract makes each of those impossible to do silently. CANCELLATION IS A STATE MACHINE WITH A DEADLINE (`running → cancelling → cancelled`, with `abandoned` when the grace passes and nobody answered), and A SECOND REQUEST DOES NOT BUY TIME: cancelling twice is idempotent, the deadline does not move and the cause is not rewritten, because a grace that grows when you ask again is a negotiation. THE RACE IS RECORDED, NOT ERASED: if the work finished after the cancellation the honest outcome is `completed-after-cancel` (with `producedOutput` a required boolean), claiming `completed` is REFUSED because it erases the cancellation, and claiming `cancelled` is refused because something did happen. A CKECKPOINT NOTICES ABANDONMENT BUT DOES NOT SETTLE IT (defect found by the first suite run: the checkpoint was writing the settlement, so the accounting could never be written afterwards) — noticing and settling are separate acts. A CANCELLED EXECUTION IS NOT FREE: what it consumed stays consumed, while the slot is returned exactly once; AN ABANDONED EXECUTION KEEPS HOLDING ITS SLOT because the ledger does not declare free what it cannot see released (that is how a pool over-subscribes itself). Charges are ADDRESSED by reference: the same reference with the same amount is a duplicate the caller may ignore, the same reference with a different amount is refused ('two amounts for one reference is two rumours for one fact'), releasing what was never charged is refused ('a slot that never existed'), releasing more than is outstanding is refused, and releasing twice is refused. Scope walls: no scheduler, queue or retry policy (P4), no slot table (P6.22 grants, this contract records), no health judgement (P6.11), no rollout (P6.19), no telemetry backend (P9); no filesystem, network, clock or randomness — every answer takes the tick it answers for and the only node import is the hash. Authority: this contract records what happened to a cancelled execution and what it cost; it never decides whether something should run and never invents a charge.

contracts.notes: P6.24 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): runtime pools. A pool is several workers that may host the same work plus the policy that decides which one does; the interesting part is not 'pick a free worker' but that a pool is where a runtime over-subscribes itself by counting only the work it can see. A PLACEMENT IS DECIDED, NOT SAMPLED: scoring is declared data (locality, warm affinity, free capacity, declared priority, then id) so the same pool and the same request always answer the same way — a placement that moves when nothing changed is a placement nobody can reproduce; the first suite run refined the documented order to what the code really does (most free capacity, then priority) and the test now states it. ANTI-AFFINITY IS ENFORCED: a pool declares how many instances of one identity may share a worker, and the next instance goes elsewhere — the refusal names the limit ('allows 1 instance(s) … per worker'). CAPACITY COUNTS WHAT THE POOL CANNOT SEE: outstanding work (slots a lease still holds, including the ones an abandoned execution kept in P6.23) is passed in as data and counts against the worker, so a request is refused with `pool.over-subscribed` and the message 'counting only what the pool placed would place work it cannot run' instead of placing work the worker cannot run. DRAINING IS NOT DELETION: a draining worker takes no new placements and keeps the work it has, and a worker with placed or outstanding work cannot be removed ('work does not vanish because a record says it did'). REBALANCING IS ADVICE: it names where the NEXT placement for a concentrated identity should go and never moves running work — moving a running execution is a cancellation and belongs to P6.23; the advice stays inside the locality the placement names (a second suite-run refinement: sending the next placement to a worker of another locality would be advice about a request nobody made), and the 'nowhere to move' case is reachable and tested. Releasing a placement is once ('releasing it twice would invent a second slot') and releasing what was never placed is refused ('would invent capacity'). contracts.notes: P6.25 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): the native ABI and dual artifacts. A node identity may be implemented twice — once in JavaScript for js-compat, once natively for rust-native — and that is only an asset if the two are THE SAME NODE, which means three things have to be true and checkable. (1) NOTHING LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC CROSSES: the boundary carries a closed set of types (null, boolean, number, string, list, map and a bytes handle), the host owns item memory, and a pointer borrowing or language object crossing would make the implementation language part of the contract, which the milestone forbids — the suite asserts the type list contains no pointer. (2) AN ARTIFACT'S LOCALITY IS NOT A FREE CHOICE: the kind decides the locality (js → js-compat, native → rust-native, wasm → wasm) and a native or WASM artifact must declare the ABI it was built against (`lego-native-abi@1`), while a js implementation claiming an ABI version is refused as a costume. (3) TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS ARE CHECKED WITH ONE SET OF VECTORS: `conformanceVectors` derives deterministic cases from the wire contract (empty item, full item, an unexpected field whose expectation depends on whether the shape is open or closed, and a null in a declared field — a value, not an absence), so both implementations are asked exactly the same questions, and the vector set carries a digest. `compareConformance` reads what each implementation actually did: A CASE THAT DID NOT RUN IS `INCOMPLETE` AND NEVER A PASS, a mismatch is `DIVERGENT` with the case and the note named. `conformDualArtifact` refuses vectors that belong to another wire contract or identity ('would prove nothing'), refuses results for an implementation the artifact does not declare, and treats an implementation that was declared but never asked as INCOMPLETE — 'a promise with a hole in it is not conformance' — with the headline rule that TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS THAT DISAGREE ARE TWO NODES SHARING A NAME. Selection runs the implementation whose locality was asked for; falling back to another locality is allowed ONLY when declared (`allowFallback`), and then the substitution is recorded rather than silent. Scope walls: no IO compilation (P6.21 — the field map arrives as data), no semantic fingerprinting (P6.9 — the digest arrives as data), no leases (P6.22), placement (P6.24), cache (P6.26) or loading; no filesystem, network, clock, randomness, WebAssembly API, dlopen or FFI — the only node import is the hash. contracts.notes: P6.26 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): the WASM compilation cache. A cache is where a wrong answer hides — fast, shared, and authoritative-sounding — so this contract is the part of the runtime that decides what a cached module is identified by, what happens when it is wrong, and what may be thrown away. THE KEY IS CONTENT AND TOOLCHAIN: artifact digest + wire contract + ABI version + toolchain, so the same artifact compiled by another engine is another object (a cache keyed by a path or 'latest' answers yesterday's question today); the suite proves a toolchain change yields a different key. A FAILED COMPILATION IS CACHED AS A FACT WITH ITS REASON (negative entries, so a broken artifact is not recompiled on every request) AND A NEW TOOLCHAIN ASKS THE QUESTION AGAIN, because the toolchain is part of the key — the suite asserts the new engine sees a miss rather than inheriting yesterday's failure. A HIT IS NOT A GUESS: every entry carries the digest of the module it holds and `verifyHit` compares it, with a tampered digest named in the message ('expected cccccccccccc… and got eeeeeeeeeeee…'). ONE KEY HOLDS ONE MODULE: an insert whose module digest differs from the entry under that key is refused ('one key holds one module'), a compiled entry without a module digest is refused ('a hit nobody can verify is a guess'), and a cached failure is refused when it carries bytes ('caching it with bytes would make the budget lie'). A MODULE IN USE IS NEVER EVICTED: eviction takes the least recently used IDLE entry, adoption counts each user, and when every entry is in use the insert is REFUSED rather than throwing away something running ('refusing the insert rather than throwing away a module that is running') — the first suite run corrected the test fixture to actually reach that state by adopting every entry. Invalidation is TARGETED (by artifact, by toolchain, or both) and leaves in-use entries until they are released; an empty selector is refused because 'clearing a cache is a restart'. Digests are presented to humans without the sha256: noise (a suite-driven readability fix). Scope walls: no compilation, no engine, no bytecode inspection, no WebAssembly API — the caller compiles and reports what happened; no artifact declaration (P6.25), leases (P6.22), placement (P6.24) or loading of bytes; no filesystem, network, clock or randomness — the only node import is the hash and every answer takes the tick it answers for. Authority: this contract decides what a cache may return and throw away; it never compiles, never executes and never decides that a module is safe to run.

contracts.notes: P6.27 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): provenance statements and the transparency log. 'Where did these bytes come from' has a cheap wrong answer — a field in a manifest, a build id, a CI badge — so this contract makes the answer cost something. PROVENANCE IS A STATEMENT ABOUT A SUBJECT DIGEST: a subject without a digest is refused as 'a rumour with a version number', a statement naming a different digest is a mismatch ('provenance about something else is not provenance about this'), and the name has to match too. EVERY INPUT IS NAMED AND DIGESTED — source, dependency, toolchain, configuration — because 'built from the repository' is not a claim this contract accepts; a material without a digest is 'an input nobody can check'; a duplicated material is refused; and a build that finished before it started is refused. A STATEMENT NOBODY HAS SEEN IS A CLAIM, NOT EVIDENCE: publication into the log is what makes verification possible, and an unpublished statement verifies as insufficient ('a statement nobody else has seen is a claim, not evidence'); the policy can waive publication, and it says so in the result. THE LOG IS APPEND-ONLY AND ITS HEAD IS A CHECKPOINT: every record links to the one before it, publishing the same statement twice is the SAME record (a log that grows when nothing happened is a log nobody can reason about), and a record rebuilt under one digest for another subject is refused. AN INCLUSION PROOF IS CHECKED, NOT TRUSTED: verifyInclusion walks the links, refuses a log that ends sooner than the proof admits ('a log that ends sooner than the proof admits is a log something was removed from'), a rebuilt record ('the log has been rebuilt differently'), a broken chain, and a proof that has been superseded by a newer head. PROVENANCE IS NOT TRUST AND PERFORMS NO CRYPTOGRAPHY: signing and attestation belong to P6.12, trust classes to P6.1, the epoch chain to P6.16 — the suite asserts this module reaches none of them (no createSign/subtle/privateKey/signAttestation, no other module of the registry), and that the only node import is the hash. No filesystem, network, clock or randomness: every record takes the tick it happened at. Authority: this contract records and checks where an artifact came from; it never decides whether it may run.

contracts.notes: P6.28 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): update metadata freshness. A valid signature says who wrote a sentence, not when the sentence stopped being true, so this contract is about the three attacks that survive verification: rollback, freeze, mix-and-match. A VERSION THAT GOES BACKWARDS IS REFUSED BY NAME ('a version that goes backwards is the attack the number exists to stop'), AND SO IS THE QUIETER VERSION OF IT — the same version arriving with different bytes, which is a fork, not an update. EXPIRY IS A VERDICT, NOT A TIMESTAMP: expired metadata says yesterday's truth and is refused rather than used ('expired metadata says yesterday's truth, so it is refused rather than used'); a declared clock skew is allowed and named in the refusal when it is exceeded; and a check at a tick EARLIER than the last check is refused as well, because 'a clock that goes backwards relative to the last check is how a freeze is hidden'. SILENCE IS NOT A SIGNATURE: signature counts are SUPPLIED by the caller (P6.12 owns crypto), metadata below the threshold is `incomplete`, and `incomplete` is not a pass — the suite proves a policy can raise the bar per role and that metadata below it is refused, and that a required role that is absent is an incomplete, named verdict rather than a pass. METADATA FROM TWO SNAPSHOTS IS ONE SNAPSHOT TOO MANY: the snapshot names the version and digest of each role below it, and a targets file that is not the one the snapshot names is a mismatch however well it verifies on its own; the suite also shows the binding can be waived explicitly and that a role named by the snapshot but not supplied is simply not in hand. A DELEGATION MAY NARROW, NEVER WIDEN: a delegated role signs inside the paths its parent covers (with the path-vs-string boundary spelled out — 'packages-other/x' is not inside 'packages/', and the directory entry 'packages' is not a path inside 'packages/'), may not delegate to itself, and may not lower the bar its parent set; a delegation that states no threshold inherits its parent's. A REFRESH IS A PLAN, NOT A FETCH: this contract has no network — it asks for the timestamp first, and when the timestamp did not move it stops, because 'asking anyway is how a freeze goes unnoticed for a year'; the suite covers stopping at the timestamp, at the snapshot, asking blind when nothing was supplied, and a policy that skips the root. THE MODULE PERFORMS NO CRYPTOGRAPHY AND TOUCHES NOTHING ELSE: no signature checking, no keys, no attestation (P6.12), no trust class (P6.1), no admission (P6.17), no epoch chain (P6.16) — the suite asserts the only node import is the hash, that no clock or network or randomness is read, and that no neighbouring module is reached into. Authority: this contract decides whether metadata is current enough to use; it never decides whether the artifact it describes may run.

contracts.notes: P6.29 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): name claims, handovers and the confusion between them. Every other contract identifies a node by type@typeVersion; this one is about the part in front of that, because a name that means two things quietly is how a dependency gets swapped for another one that runs. A CLAIM IS MADE BY KEY, NOT BY SPELLING: 'Some-Node' and 'some-node' are one name, a second claim under a name already claimed is refused ('a second claim is a handover or a confusion, never a quiet overwrite'), and a second spelling is refused as a fold ('two spellings of one name are one name'); nothing is written when a claim is refused. A NAME THAT NEEDS A SECOND LOOK IS A NAME THAT LIES: anything outside ASCII is refused with the code point and its position named (U+2011 at position 3, U+00DC at position 0), whitespace inside or around a name is refused, scoped names must have a scope and a name ('a scope is not a package'), a slash without a scope is refused, and a name past the 214-character limit is refused. A NAME ONE EDIT FROM ANOTHER IS A CONFUSION: distance is computed in edits with transposition counted as one ('a transposition is one edit, and it is the cheapest confusion there is'), an unknown name within reach of a name somebody else holds is refused as a typosquat, while the SAME NEAR NEIGHBOUR BELONGS TO ITS OWN HOLDER is a relative rather than a swap and resolves as a new name; the reach is stated by policy rather than assumed, and a policy of zero edits is refused because looking for a confusion with no edits allowed is looking for the exact name. A NAME THAT CHANGES HANDS QUIETLY IS REFUSED: resolving a known name to another publisher is name-reused ('a name that changes hands quietly is how a dependency is swapped'); with a declared handover it resolves as handover, BEFORE the declared tick it is refused ('a handover does not travel backwards'), it does not come back to the publisher that handed it over, and a third publisher arriving is not a handover. A HANDOVER IS AN ACCUSATION UNTIL IT IS EVIDENCED: it names who holds the name ('a handover from somebody who does not hold the name is a wish'), who takes it, when, and on what grounds ('without evidence is a rumour with a timestamp'), and it cannot go backwards past the claim or an earlier handover. VISIBILITY IS PART OF THE NAME: a public claim does not answer a private name ('the public registry answering a private name is the oldest confusion there is') and the reverse is refused too. Reads: describeNamespace is a census of claims, publishers, handovers and private names; explainNamespace renders the decision; every decision carries a digest over its own inputs so the same question at the same tick gives the same answer. Scope walls: no workflow resolution (P6.14), no epoch (P6.16), no admission (P6.17), no freshness (P6.28), no trust class (P6.1); no filesystem, network, clock or randomness, and the only node import is the hash. Authority: this contract decides whether a name is the name that was meant; it never decides whether the node behind it may run.

contracts.notes: P6.30 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): repair assessment, ordered restoration and offline recovery. A registry comes back from an interrupted install, a lost file, a machine that has been offline for a month, and the two ways to get this wrong are to trust what is there and to repair what is not. A DAMAGED REGISTRY IS COMPARED, NOT TRUSTED: an expectation (what should be there, by digest) is compared with a census (what is there, by digest) and the answer is a NAMED census of damage — intact, altered, missing, unexpected ('1 altered, 1 missing and 1 unexpected item(s) against 3 expected'); an empty expectation is refused because 'a repair with nothing to compare against is a wish'. AN ITEM THAT DOES NOT HASH TO ITS OWN DIGEST IS NOT EVIDENCE: bytes supplied with a census are hashed here and a self-inconsistent item is refused by digest prefix rather than folded in; a census with no items is still a census, because that is how a wiped install looks. A REPAIR DOES NOT DELETE WHAT IT DID NOT PUT THERE: an unexpected item is quarantined and named, never deleted, because its presence is not evidence of damage to another file — and the suite asserts no step anywhere is a delete. OFFLINE IS A DECISION AND IT IS THE DEFAULT: a plan is offline unless the caller says otherwise, an offline repair may not use a mirror ('this repair is offline and the only source for c is a mirror'), and the online case says so in the plan and in the message; this contract has no network at all — the caller names the sources. A REPAIR CANNOT INVENT CONTENT IT HAS NEVER SEEN: an item is restored from a named source or the plan is BLOCKED BY NAME ('nothing has the bytes for b'), and blocked items are never quietly dropped from a plan that still looks successful. RESTORATION FOLLOWS DEPENDENCIES, NOT ALPHABET: the order is topological with an alphabetical tie-break, a dependency outside the set being repaired is not part of the order, and a cycle is refused rather than broken at random ('a cycle is not an order: a, b are waiting on each other'). REPAIRING AN EPOCH THAT HAS BEEN SUPERSEDED IS A ROLLBACK WEARING A RECOVERY'S CLOTHES: when the caller names the superseded epochs, a census sitting on one is refused outright and NO PARTIAL PLAN IS PRODUCED. PART OF THE WAY BACK IS NOT BACK: verifyRepair decides separately from the plan, names the items that still do not match, and says how far short the registry is. Scope walls: no artefact store (P6.7), no epoch chain (P6.16), no admission (P6.17), no freshness (P6.28), no names or trust (P6.29, P6.1) — the suite asserts the only node import is the hash, that no clock or network or randomness is read, and that no neighbouring module is reached into. Authority: this contract decides what is missing and what may be put back; it never fetches and never decides whether the restored registry may serve.

contracts.notes: P6.31 (P6 implementation owner: Agent 3, Issue #100): the acceptance of the milestone, and deliberately the least powerful contract of the lane. It composes the verdicts of the other contracts AS DATA — it never imports, re-runs or overrules them — and its answer is allowed to be 'not proven'. A CRITERION IS A CLAIM WITH A KIND, A SLICE, A COMMIT, A VERDICT AND EVIDENCE: the kinds are the ones the lane promised per slice (focused, negative, boundary, determinism, security, resource, rollback, docs, evidence), a criterion outside those kinds is refused, and a milestone that has no negative criterion has not been tested, only exercised. A PASS WITH NOTHING TO POINT AT IS AN OPINION: 'pass' and 'fail' both require an evidence digest ('a criterion without evidence is an opinion with a verdict attached'), while 'incomplete' is the verdict for the absence of evidence and is exactly what it is for. NOT APPLICABLE IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE SUBJECT, so it has to say why, and A KIND COVERED ONLY BY NOT-APPLICABLE CRITERIA IS NOT COVERED — the suite proves a kind whose only criterion is not-applicable lands in missingKinds rather than counting as coverage. AN OMISSION IS NOT A SMALLER MILESTONE: a missing slice, an undeclared slice, a criterion checked on another commit and an uncovered kind are all findings, and A CRITERION CHECKED ON ANOTHER COMMIT COVERS NOTHING HERE, so it cannot stand in for a slice's evidence; findings are COLLECTED rather than short-circuited, because a milestone that fails four ways should say four things. THE WEAKEST VERDICT GOVERNS: a failure is a fact and an incomplete is an absence, and a milestone reporting both is rejected with the failures named. A LANE CANNOT ACCEPT ITSELF: verifiedBy must differ from implementedBy and the refusal names both ('a lane cannot accept itself'), and A MILESTONE IS ACCEPTED ON THE INTEGRATION RATHER THAN ON THE BRANCH: protected-main is false until it is reported, and an unreported integration makes the verdict incomplete, never accepted. A narrowed kind set is possible but has to be DECLARED through policy, and narrowing the kinds does not narrow the slices. Reads: describeAcceptance is a census (passed over covered slices, findings), explainAcceptance renders the report, and every report carries a digest over its own body so the same evidence at the same subject gives the same answer while another subject is another report. Scope walls: it does not run acceptance (P6.15 owns the slice-level runner), does not decide trust (P6.1), admission (P6.17), epochs (P6.16) or repair (P6.30), imports no other module of this repository, and reads no filesystem, network, clock or randomness — the only node import is the hash. Authority: this contract decides whether the evidence for a milestone adds up; it does not merge, it does not declare the lane integrated, and it cannot make a failing criterion pass.

P5.1 security kernel. Immutable PrincipalSnapshot, request-local SecurityContext and the versioned SecurityStamp that decides whether cached authority is still CURRENT, must be RE_EVALUATEd, or is DENY. Performs no I/O: no network, no filesystem, no decryption. Holds no secret material and no user profile - the constructor rejects unknown fields so a stored user record cannot ride into the execution path. SecurityError refuses any code not published in contracts/errors.contract.json (foundation F16 by construction). Introduces ZERO new error codes. Deliberately NOT authentication, NOT an authorization engine (P5.3), NOT a credential path (P5.4), NOT a second capability engine: plugin policy stays in src/lego/plugin-policy.mjs. auth.identity@1.0.0 is unchanged and remains a read-only projection.

contracts.notes: P5.2 session kernel + CSRF boundary. Revocable server-side session records replacing the previously unrevocable stateless bearer token: token payload changed from {sub,iat,exp} to {sid,ver,exp} so authority lives in a record that can be killed. Rotation kills the old token immediately (fixation + replay defence); revoke/revokeAll; per-user securityVersion invalidation; bounded absolute and idle lifetimes with the absolute deadline never sliding. Session store is process-local and bounded, so a restart invalidates everything and a session flood costs bounded memory. CSRF combines Origin/Referer validation with a session-bound double-submit token; safe methods and session-less requests are exempt. No MFA, no API keys, no password reset, no credential encryption (P5.6/P5.7/P5.4). No distributed consensus. Introduces ZERO new error codes.

P5.3 authorization engine, resource policy and versioned decision cache. Default-deny evaluation over principal + tenant + action + resourceType + resourceId + capability + policyVersion. Authority is never inferred from authentication, UI visibility, plugin trust, language or provider existence. The permission universe is DERIVED from the extracted pinned-n8n role model (data/roles.json via compat/scopes.mjs) and compiled to dense numeric ids for the hot path - no second authorization vocabulary. CRITICAL invariant: an unknown permission or scope fails CLOSED (SECURITY_REASON.UNKNOWN_PERMISSION) rather than matching nothing silently. The decision cache is bounded and version-aware: every entry is stamped, and a stale entry is DROPPED and re-evaluated, so the cache can never serve a decision computed under older authority - the cache is an optimization, versions are correctness. Approval and step-up are INPUTS, not local logic (P5.6 owns approval; P5.1 owns the strength ladder). No I/O: no network, no filesystem, no decryption. Holds no credential material. Session, credential vault, KMS, MFA and API-key storage are all non-scope.

P5.5 provider-neutral credential crypto. KeyProvider contract (currentKeyRef/readableKeyRefs/deriveKey/fingerprint/beginRotation/abortRotation/retire/state) with a local-file (0600, atomic) and a memory provider; key lineage; controlled read window of current + at most one previous; HKDF per-purpose subkeys; retire destroys material. Versioned AES-256-GCM envelope whose AAD binds cryptoVersion, tenantId, credentialId, type and keyRef; wrong key, tamper and substitution are one indistinguishable authentication-failed. Vault: seal/open with NO plaintext fallback; metadata and non-secret config stay clear, only the runtime secret is sealed; verified incremental re-encryption committed per batch; resumable rotation, recover() on boot, rollback-safe abort; one-time legacy plaintext migration; recovery metadata without material; encrypted backup manifest; quarantined restore validated in full before one atomic commit. Every failure fails closed with an existing published error code. No master/root key in credential records. External KMS, distributed consensus, billing and P10 provisioning are non-scope.

P5.6 account security primitives, HTTP-free (the boundary is src/auth/account-routes.mjs on the upstream n8n wire contract). abuse-control: fixed-window rate limiters and capped exponential failure back-off, every table bounded (maxKeys) with reclaim-then-degrade into a shared overflow bucket, keys are HMAC digests; limits reproduce the pinned upstream decorators. password-hash: scrypt with algorithm agility and rehash-on-success; the current policy equals the legacy parameters and keeps the legacy format for rollback safety; unknown accounts spend equal scrypt cost; upstream passwordSchema messages. reset-token: 256-bit single-use tokens, digest-only storage, 20 min default and 1 h hard cap, one live token per user, bound to a credential fingerprint, bounded table. mfa: RFC 6238 TOTP (otpauth defaults), step replay refusal, recovery codes as SHA-256 digests consumed on use, explicit state machine, and a collection view that keeps sealed TOTP secrets on the P5.5 vault key lineage. step-up: declared strength per sensitive operation on the P5.1 AUTH_STRENGTHS ladder; interactive sessions only.

contracts.notes: P5.7 machine identity, HTTP-free and storage-free (the boundary is src/auth/api-key-routes.mjs: upstream /rest/api-keys wire contract plus authenticateMachineCredential). api-key: 256-bit keys shown once; only a SHA-256 digest and a 4-character hint are stored (pinned n8n stores the raw JWT); the owner id inside the key gives an O(1) lookup with no process-local index; lifecycle verdicts (revoked, expired in unix seconds, owner unavailable, audience mismatch); scope attenuation reports escalation instead of trimming; effective scopes are re-intersected with the owner's current grant on every use. machine-identity: service principals (worker, agent, mcp, gateway) with their own credential and audience, bound to the owner's tenant; agent delegation that is a subset of the parent, never outlives it, never crosses tenants, never exceeds the parent's auth strength and is depth-bounded; a validated tenant security policy input; the authority chain principal -> P5.3 authorize -> approval input -> ai.approval evaluate (injected port, fail closed; P5 is not the approval engine); audit events with reference and reason fields only. The API-key scope vocabulary is extracted from the pinned @n8n/permissions source into data/api-key-scopes.json (compat/api-key-scopes.mjs mirrors upstream getApiKeyScopesForRole).
